groups.everyday: Everyday or popular terms (not DSM diagnoses)

terms.plain_definition: Not being able to enjoy things you used to like. Food, music, friends, hobbies all feel flat or pointless.
terms.everyday_example: Your favourite show is on and you just stare at it, feeling nothing, then switch it off.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It isn't laziness or being ungrateful. The 'enjoy' switch is stuck, and it can come back with treatment.

terms.plain_definition: A feeling of being disconnected from yourself, your body, your memories, or the world around you. It can be mild, like daydreaming, or strong enough to lose time.
terms.everyday_example: You drive home and can't remember any of the journey, or during a scary moment you feel like you're watching yourself from outside.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Mild dissociation is common and normal. It becomes a problem when it happens often, lasts a long time, or gets in the way of life.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Feeling like the world around you isn't real. Things can look foggy, flat, dreamlike, or far away.
terms.everyday_example: Walking down your own street and feeling like it's a film set or a dream.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Derealization is frightening but not dangerous, and it doesn't mean you're 'losing your mind'. It's often linked to stress, anxiety, or lack of sleep.

terms.plain_definition: Feeling detached from your own body, thoughts, or feelings, as if you're watching yourself from outside or you're a robot going through the motions.
terms.everyday_example: Looking in the mirror and the face doesn't feel like yours, even though you know it is.
terms.common_misunderstanding: People experiencing this know it's a feeling, not reality. That's what makes it different from psychosis.

terms.plain_definition: A period of unusually high energy, confidence, and fast thinking, with less need for sleep. It's milder than mania and doesn't involve losing touch with reality.
terms.everyday_example: Four days of sleeping three hours a night, starting five projects, talking faster than usual, and friends saying 'you're not yourself'.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Hypomania can feel great, so people often don't see it as a problem. Treatment aims for steady mood, not for taking away energy or creativity.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: A period of very high or irritable mood and energy that lasts at least a week, is clearly out of character, and causes serious problems. It can include risky decisions and, sometimes, losing touch with reality.
terms.everyday_example: Spending savings in a weekend, feeling chosen for a special mission, and not sleeping for days.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Mania isn't 'just being happy'. It can be frightening for the person and for the people around them, and it needs medical care.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: When symptoms of depression and mania or hypomania happen at the same time, like feeling wired and hopeless at once.
terms.everyday_example: Racing thoughts and restless energy, but everything feels dark and pointless.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Mixed states can be especially distressing and are linked with higher risk, so they deserve quick attention, not waiting it out.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: When the mind loses touch with what's real for a time. It can mean hearing or seeing things others don't, or believing things that aren't true, even with strong evidence.
terms.everyday_example: Hearing a voice commenting on what you do when nobody is there, and feeling sure the TV is sending you messages.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Psychosis is a symptom, not a personality. About 3 in 100 people experience it at some point, and most recover well, especially with early help.

terms.plain_definition: A firm belief that isn't true and doesn't change even with clear evidence against it. Common themes include being watched, being special, or being harmed.
terms.everyday_example: Being certain that the neighbours have planted cameras, despite searching the house and finding nothing.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Arguing someone out of a delusion rarely works and can hurt the relationship. Staying calm and focusing on their feelings helps more.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: Sensing something that isn't there: hearing, seeing, smelling, tasting, or feeling it. Hearing voices is the most common kind.
terms.everyday_example: Hearing someone say your name clearly when you're alone in the house.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Hallucinations happen in many situations, including grief, fever, drug use, and falling asleep. On their own they don't mean someone has schizophrenia.

terms.plain_definition: Hearing speech or sounds that other people can't hear. Voices can be kind, neutral, or cruel, and some people live well with them.
terms.everyday_example: A voice that comments on what you're doing, or several voices talking about you.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Many voice-hearers are not ill and never need treatment. When voices are distressing, support groups and therapy can help as much as medication.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Feeling suspicious or threatened by others when there isn't good reason. It ranges from everyday wariness to fixed, frightening beliefs.
terms.everyday_example: Feeling sure that colleagues are plotting against you after a normal meeting.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Mild suspicious thoughts are common, especially under stress. 'Paranoid' is not a word to throw at someone who is just careful.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: An unwanted thought, image, or urge that keeps coming back, causes anxiety, and feels impossible to ignore. In OCD it's the 'O'.
terms.everyday_example: A constant fear that you left the stove on, even after checking, and the thought won't go away.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Being 'obsessed' with a band is enthusiasm. A clinical obsession is unwanted, distressing, and not about enjoyment.

terms.plain_definition: An action, or a mental act like counting, that a person feels driven to repeat to ease anxiety or stop something bad from happening. In OCD it's the 'C'.
terms.everyday_example: Checking the door lock exactly eight times before you can leave, and starting over if you lose count.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Compulsions aren't habits or quirks. They bring short relief, then the anxiety comes back stronger, which is why treatment focuses on breaking the cycle.

terms.plain_definition: Having more than one condition at the same time, like depression and anxiety, or ADHD and a learning difference.
terms.everyday_example: Being treated for anxiety and finding out you also have ADHD, which explains why some things never got easier.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Having two diagnoses doesn't mean you're 'twice as broken'. It's very common, and treatments often help both.

terms.plain_definition: A period when symptoms have mostly or fully gone. Partial remission means some symptoms remain; full remission means none that cause trouble.
terms.everyday_example: After months of treatment, you notice you've gone weeks without a low day.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Remission isn't the same as 'cured', and it isn't failure if symptoms return. Many people have long remissions with the right support.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: When symptoms come back after a period of feeling better. For substance use it means returning to use after stopping.
terms.everyday_example: Feeling well for a year, then a stressful job change brings the old symptoms back.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A relapse is a bump in the road, not a reset to zero. Everything learned before still counts.

sources.title: Drugs, Brains, and Behavior: The Science of Addiction

terms.plain_definition: The early stage before a condition fully shows itself, when small changes appear, like sleeping less, pulling away from friends, or thinking differently.
terms.everyday_example: In the months before a first psychotic episode, someone becomes withdrawn and suspicious without knowing why.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Noticing a prodrome is a chance to get help early, not proof that something terrible will happen.

terms.plain_definition: The emotion a person shows on the outside, in their face, voice, and body. 'Flat affect' means showing very little emotion, even when feeling it inside.
terms.everyday_example: Someone describes their father's death in a steady voice with no expression, though they're deeply sad.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Flat affect doesn't mean a person doesn't care. Depression, some medications, and schizophrenia can all dampen how feelings show.

terms.plain_definition: How much a person recognizes that what they're experiencing is part of a condition. Insight can be full, partial, or absent, and it can change over time.
terms.everyday_example: Someone in a manic episode feels wonderful and doesn't believe anything is wrong.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Low insight isn't stubbornness or denial. In some conditions the brain itself makes it hard to see the change.

terms.plain_definition: A condition where the brain cannot recognize its own illness. The person genuinely doesn't see that anything is wrong. It's common in psychosis and dementia.
terms.everyday_example: A grandmother insists she's fine living alone, although she's forgotten to eat for days.
terms.common_misunderstanding: This is not denial or pride. Arguing doesn't fix it; building trust and working around it does.

terms.plain_definition: The brain's 'management team': planning, starting tasks, remembering steps, controlling impulses, and switching between things.
terms.everyday_example: Knowing exactly what you need to do, staring at it for an hour, and not being able to start.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Struggling with executive function isn't a character flaw. It's a brain-based difference that tools and support can help with.

terms.plain_definition: When executive function isn't working well: trouble starting, organizing, finishing, or switching tasks, even ones you want to do.
terms.everyday_example: The dishes sit there for days. You want to do them. You just can't make yourself begin.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It looks like laziness from outside and feels like a wall from inside. Breaking tasks into tiny steps and using outside structure helps.

terms.plain_definition: The mental notepad that holds information for a few seconds while you use it, like a phone number you're about to dial.
terms.everyday_example: Walking into a room and forgetting why, or losing the thread of a sentence halfway through.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Weak working memory isn't low intelligence. Many very bright people have it, especially with ADHD.

terms.plain_definition: Thinking skills: attention, memory, language, reasoning, and problem-solving. 'Cognitive symptoms' means changes in these.
terms.everyday_example: Depression can make reading a page three times feel necessary because nothing sticks.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Cognitive' doesn't mean 'intelligent'. It just means 'to do with thinking'.

terms.plain_definition: A habit of thinking that twists reality, like assuming the worst or seeing things as all good or all bad. Everyone has some; they get louder when we're low or anxious.
terms.everyday_example: One friend doesn't text back and your mind says, 'Nobody likes me.'
terms.common_misunderstanding: Noticing a distortion doesn't mean your feelings are wrong. It means the thought may not be the whole truth.

terms.plain_definition: Jumping to the worst possible outcome and believing it's likely. A common thinking trap in anxiety.
terms.everyday_example: A headache becomes 'what if it's a brain tumour' within minutes.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Catastrophizing is a habit the mind learns to feel prepared. It can be unlearned.

terms.plain_definition: Staying away from places, people, thoughts, or feelings that cause anxiety or bring back painful memories. It brings relief now and makes the fear bigger later.
terms.everyday_example: Taking a 40-minute detour every day so you never have to cross the bridge where you panicked once.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Avoidance makes sense; it feels protective. But facing feared things slowly, with support, is how fear shrinks.

terms.plain_definition: Something that sets off a strong reaction linked to a past experience or a condition: a smell, a sound, a place, a date, a tone of voice.
terms.everyday_example: Fireworks bringing a veteran straight back to a war zone in their body.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Online, 'triggered' is often used to mean 'annoyed'. The clinical meaning is a sudden, overwhelming reaction the person didn't choose.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Suddenly feeling like a past traumatic event is happening again, right now. It can involve images, sounds, smells, body sensations, or just intense emotion.
terms.everyday_example: A car backfires and for a few seconds you're back in the crash, heart pounding, unable to tell where you are.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Flashbacks aren't 'just memories'. The brain and body react as if the danger is present, which is why grounding techniques help.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: A sudden wave of old feelings, like shame, terror, or abandonment, without a clear picture of the past event. Common after long-term childhood trauma.
terms.everyday_example: A mild criticism at work and you feel tiny, worthless, and terrified for the rest of the day.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Because there's no 'movie', people often don't realize it's trauma-related and blame themselves for overreacting.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Being constantly on guard for danger: scanning rooms, jumping at noises, finding it hard to relax or sleep.
terms.everyday_example: Always sitting with your back to the wall and knowing where every exit is.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's the body's alarm system stuck on, not paranoia or drama.

terms.plain_definition: Jumping or flinching far more than usual at sudden noises or touch.
terms.everyday_example: A friend taps your shoulder and you nearly hit the ceiling, heart racing for minutes after.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's a reflex, not a choice, and it often settles as trauma treatment progresses.

terms.plain_definition: Feeling cut off from emotions, including good ones. Common after trauma and in depression; it's the mind turning the volume down to cope.
terms.everyday_example: Your best friend announces she's engaged and you feel like you're hearing it through glass.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Numbness isn't 'not caring'. It's often the mind protecting itself, and feelings can return, sometimes with support to handle them.

terms.plain_definition: Memories of a frightening event that push into your mind without warning, often with strong emotion or body sensations.
terms.everyday_example: Doing homework and suddenly the image of the accident is there, as vivid as the day it happened.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Trying to push these memories away usually makes them come back harder. Trauma therapies teach a different approach.

terms.plain_definition: Body symptoms, like pain, tiredness, dizziness, or stomach trouble, that are real and can be linked to stress or emotions.
terms.everyday_example: Stomach aches every Sunday night before school, with nothing found on medical tests.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Psychosomatic' doesn't mean 'imaginary'. The pain is real; the mind and body are one system.

terms.plain_definition: Real symptoms like weakness, shaking, blackouts, or numbness caused by a problem in how the nervous system works, not by damage to it. Like software, not hardware.
terms.everyday_example: Legs that won't move on some days, with normal scans, that improve with specialist physiotherapy.
terms.common_misunderstanding: People with FND are often told it's 'all in their head'. It isn't. It's a recognized, treatable condition.

terms.plain_definition: A sudden, fast, repeated movement or sound that's hard to control, like blinking, shoulder jerks, sniffing, or throat clearing.
terms.everyday_example: Noticing you've been clearing your throat every few seconds since a stressful week started.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Tics are not attention-seeking or bad habits, and most children's tics fade with time.

terms.plain_definition: Repeating words or phrases you've heard, right away or later. It's common in autism and can be a way of communicating or self-soothing.
terms.everyday_example: A child answers 'Do you want juice?' with 'Do you want juice?', meaning yes.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Echolalia is often meaningful communication, not 'just copying'.

terms.plain_definition: Repeated movements or sounds, like rocking, hand-flapping, humming, or fidgeting, that help regulate feelings and senses. Everyone stims a bit; autistic people often stim more.
terms.everyday_example: Flapping your hands when you're excited, or rocking when the room is too loud.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Stimming is usually helpful and harmless. Stopping someone from stimming often makes things worse, not better.

terms.plain_definition: Experiencing sounds, lights, textures, smells, or touch much more (or less) strongly than most people. Common in autism and ADHD.
terms.everyday_example: A clothing label feels like sandpaper, or the hum of fluorescent lights makes it impossible to concentrate.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not fussiness. The nervous system really is processing input differently.

terms.plain_definition: Sensing what's going on inside your body: hunger, thirst, needing the toilet, a racing heart, feeling anxious. Some people feel these signals very strongly, others barely at all.
terms.everyday_example: Not noticing you were hungry until you feel shaky and irritable.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Low interoception can make it hard to name feelings, which can be mistaken for 'not caring'.

terms.plain_definition: Difficulty noticing, naming, and describing your own emotions. You feel something, but can't tell what.
terms.everyday_example: Someone asks how you feel about the breakup and the honest answer is 'I don't know, tense?'
terms.common_misunderstanding: People with alexithymia do have feelings. They just struggle to read them, and it can be learned slowly with help.

terms.plain_definition: When thoughts become jumbled, jump between unrelated topics, or are hard for others to follow. A symptom in some psychotic episodes.
terms.everyday_example: Answering a question about lunch with a long string of loosely connected ideas that trail off.
terms.common_misunderstanding: The person is not being difficult. Their thoughts really are harder to organize, and this usually improves with treatment.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: In psychosis, the things that are 'taken away': motivation, energy, expression, speech, and pleasure. They're often harder to treat than voices or delusions.
terms.everyday_example: Sitting all day, speaking in short answers, not because of sadness but because the drive is gone.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Negative symptoms are often mistaken for laziness or depression. They are part of the illness.

terms.plain_definition: In psychosis, the things that are 'added': hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking. 'Positive' here means present, not good.
terms.everyday_example: Hearing voices and believing you're being followed are both positive symptoms.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Positive symptoms usually respond best to antipsychotic medication.

terms.plain_definition: Feeling that ordinary things, like a song on the radio or a stranger's glance, are secretly about you or meant for you.
terms.everyday_example: Being sure the newsreader paused on purpose to send you a signal.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Fleeting self-conscious thoughts like this are common in everyone. It's a concern when they're constant and firmly believed.

terms.plain_definition: An inflated sense of being special, powerful, or important, far beyond what the facts support. It can appear in mania and in some personality patterns.
terms.everyday_example: Believing you'll be a billionaire by Friday and quitting your job to prepare.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Grandiosity in a manic episode is a symptom, not arrogance. The person usually returns to their normal self.

terms.plain_definition: Talking fast, loudly, and continuously, as if the words are pushing to get out, with little room for others to speak.
terms.everyday_example: A friend calls at 2 a.m. and talks for an hour without pausing, jumping from topic to topic.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's a recognizable sign of hypomania or mania, not just being chatty or excited.

terms.plain_definition: Thoughts coming so fast you can't keep up, hopping from one idea to the next. Happens in mania, severe anxiety, and sometimes when very sleep-deprived.
terms.everyday_example: Lying in bed with ten ideas at once and no way to slow them down.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Racing thoughts in mania feel exciting; in anxiety they feel frightening. Both are worth mentioning to a clinician.

terms.plain_definition: Visible changes in how the body moves because of mood: pacing, wringing hands, and restlessness (agitation), or moving and speaking very slowly (slowing).
terms.everyday_example: Everything feels like wading through treacle, and it takes a minute to answer a simple question.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Psychomotor slowing is a real physical sign of depression, not 'being slow' or lazy.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: Fast, strong mood shifts, often triggered by small things, that settle within hours rather than days.
terms.everyday_example: Going from content to furious to tearful in one afternoon, then wondering what happened.
terms.common_misunderstanding: This is not the same as bipolar disorder, where mood episodes last days to weeks. The two are often confused.

terms.plain_definition: Being easily annoyed, short-tempered, or on edge. In children and teens, depression and anxiety often show up as irritability rather than sadness.
terms.everyday_example: A teenager who snaps at everyone and slams doors may be struggling, not 'just being difficult'.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Irritability is a symptom worth taking seriously, especially when it's new or constant.

terms.plain_definition: A deep sense of unease, unhappiness, or discomfort. It's the opposite of euphoria. It can be about mood in general, or about a specific thing, like gender.
terms.everyday_example: A heavy, restless 'wrongness' that sits with you all day.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Dysphoria' on its own is a feeling, not a diagnosis.

terms.plain_definition: A normal, steady mood: not high, not low. For people with bipolar disorder, 'euthymic' is the goal between episodes.
terms.everyday_example: Weeks of ordinary ups and downs, nothing dramatic, sleep and energy steady.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Euthymia isn't 'boring' or 'flat'. It's the full range of normal feeling, without the extremes.

terms.plain_definition: In bipolar disorder, having four or more mood episodes in a year.
terms.everyday_example: Depressed in spring, hypomanic in June, depressed again by August, high in November.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Rapid cycling doesn't mean moods change within a day. That's a different pattern.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: When depression (or, less often, mania) reliably starts and ends at the same time of year, usually worse in autumn and winter.
terms.everyday_example: Every October the energy drains away, and every April it comes back.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Seasonal affective disorder' isn't a separate diagnosis in DSM-5-TR; it's a pattern of depression or bipolar disorder. Light therapy is one treatment.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: A mood episode that starts during pregnancy or in the weeks after birth. Depression, anxiety, and, rarely, psychosis can all happen in this window.
terms.everyday_example: Three weeks after the baby arrives, you can't stop crying and feel sure you're a terrible parent.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Perinatal depression is common, nobody's fault, and very treatable. It's different from the brief 'baby blues'.

terms.plain_definition: Tearfulness, mood swings, and feeling overwhelmed in the first two weeks after birth. Very common and usually passes on its own.
terms.everyday_example: Crying at a nappy advert on day four and laughing about it on day ten.
terms.common_misunderstanding: If low mood lasts beyond two weeks, gets worse, or includes scary thoughts, it may be perinatal depression and deserves help.

terms.plain_definition: A rare but serious condition in the days or weeks after birth, with confusion, severe mood swings, and losing touch with reality. It is a medical emergency and treatable.
terms.everyday_example: A new mother who hasn't slept in days becomes convinced of things that aren't true and is behaving very out of character.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not a sign of being a bad parent. Fast treatment leads to full recovery for most people.

terms.plain_definition: An extra label a clinician adds to a diagnosis to describe it more precisely, like 'with anxious distress' or 'in partial remission'.
terms.everyday_example: 'Major depressive disorder, recurrent, moderate, with seasonal pattern.'
terms.common_misunderstanding: Specifiers help match treatment to the person. They aren't extra diagnoses.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: The process of working out which of several possible conditions best explains what's happening, by ruling things in and out.
terms.everyday_example: Tiredness and low mood could be depression, thyroid trouble, anaemia, or sleep apnea, so a doctor checks for each.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A long first assessment is a good sign: the clinician is being careful, not doubting you.

terms.plain_definition: A 'best guess for now' diagnosis, used when the picture isn't clear yet. It's expected to be reviewed.
terms.everyday_example: 'Provisional: bipolar II' written on a letter while the team watches how mood changes over months.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A provisional diagnosis isn't a mistake or a sign of being dismissed. It's honest uncertainty.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: Needing more of a substance to get the same effect, or getting less effect from the same amount, because the body has adapted.
terms.everyday_example: Two drinks used to relax you; now it takes five.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Tolerance is a sign the body is adapting, not a sign of 'handling it well'.

sources.title: Drugs, Brains, and Behavior: The Science of Addiction
DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: The physical and emotional symptoms that appear when someone cuts down or stops a substance their body has got used to. Some withdrawals need medical supervision.
terms.everyday_example: Shaking, sweating, and anxiety the morning after not drinking for the first time in years.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Stopping some substances suddenly can be dangerous. Talk to a doctor before stopping alcohol, benzodiazepines, or opioids.

sources.title: Drugs, Brains, and Behavior: The Science of Addiction

terms.plain_definition: A strong urge or desire to use a substance or do a behaviour like gambling. Cravings usually peak and pass within minutes to an hour.
terms.everyday_example: Driving past the old pub and feeling the pull in your chest.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Having a craving isn't failure. 'Surfing' the urge until it passes is a skill that gets stronger with practice.

sources.title: Drugs, Brains, and Behavior: The Science of Addiction

terms.plain_definition: When the body has adapted to a substance so that stopping causes withdrawal. It can happen with prescribed medicines taken correctly, and isn't the same as addiction.
terms.everyday_example: Someone taking a prescribed painkiller for a year will likely need to taper off slowly, even though they never misused it.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Dependence is physical. Addiction (a use disorder) involves loss of control and continued use despite harm. People mix these up constantly.

sources.title: Drugs, Brains, and Behavior: The Science of Addiction

terms.plain_definition: The temporary changes in thinking, mood, and behaviour while a substance is active in the body.
terms.everyday_example: Being drunk is alcohol intoxication.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Intoxication on its own isn't a use disorder. A use disorder is about an ongoing pattern and its effects on life.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: Taking enough of a substance to cause serious harm, such as stopping breathing. It is a medical emergency: call your local emergency number.
terms.everyday_example: A friend who has taken something can't be woken and is breathing slowly.
terms.common_misunderstanding: People who overdose are not 'choosing' to die; many overdoses are accidental. Naloxone can reverse opioid overdoses.

terms.plain_definition: Consuming a large amount in a short time while feeling unable to stop. Used for eating and for drinking.
terms.everyday_example: Eating far past full, fast and alone, and feeling out of control while it happens.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A binge is about loss of control, not greed or weak will. Shame makes it worse; support makes it better.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: Limiting how much, how often, or what kinds of food you eat in a way that harms health, driven by fear, rules, or distress.
terms.everyday_example: Skipping meals and following rigid food rules until it takes over the day.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Restriction isn't 'discipline'. It is a symptom, and the body and brain can't recover without enough food.

terms.plain_definition: Trying to 'undo' eating through harmful means. Purging damages the body and does not do what people hope it does.
terms.everyday_example: After eating, feeling a frantic need to get rid of it.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Purging is a sign of an eating disorder, not a 'weight-control method'. Help is available and recovery is possible.

terms.plain_definition: How you see, think, and feel about your body. It can be very different from how others see you.
terms.everyday_example: Looking in the mirror and seeing something very different from what friends describe.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Poor body image is common and doesn't mean someone has an eating disorder, but it's a risk factor worth taking seriously.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Thinking about death, wishing you weren't here, or thinking about ending your life. It ranges from vague wishes to specific plans. Many people have these thoughts and come through them.
terms.everyday_example: Thinking 'everyone would be better off without me' during a bad week.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Asking someone directly about suicidal thoughts does not plant the idea. It opens the door to help. If you're having these thoughts, please reach out to a crisis line now.

terms.plain_definition: 'Passive' means wishing you weren't alive or wouldn't wake up, without planning to act. 'Active' means thinking about actually ending your life. Both matter and both deserve support.
terms.everyday_example: 'I wouldn't mind if a bus hit me' is passive; thinking about how and when is active.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Passive thoughts are not 'nothing'. They're a sign of real pain and a reason to talk to someone.

terms.plain_definition: Hurting yourself on purpose as a way to cope with overwhelming feelings. It's often not about wanting to die, though it raises risk and deserves care.
terms.everyday_example: Using pain to feel something, or to feel less, when emotions are too much.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Self-harm is not 'attention-seeking'. Most people hide it. Kindness and non-judgement help more than alarm.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: A person who has survived a suicide attempt. Many go on to live full lives and some become peer supporters for others.
terms.everyday_example: Someone who attempted at 19 and now, at 40, runs a support group.
terms.common_misunderstanding: An attempt is not a 'cry for attention' or a sign of weakness. It's a sign of unbearable pain, which can be treated.

terms.plain_definition: A person whose loved one died by suicide. This grief is often complicated by shock, guilt, and stigma, and has its own support groups.
terms.everyday_example: A parent who has lost a child to suicide and finds the only people who understand are others who have too.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Say 'died by suicide', not 'committed suicide'. The old phrase treats a death from illness like a crime.

terms.plain_definition: Things that make a mental health problem more likely (risk factors), like trauma or isolation, and things that help protect against it, like close relationships and purpose.
terms.everyday_example: A strong friendship group is a protective factor; losing a job is a risk factor.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Risk factors raise the odds; they don't decide the outcome. Protective factors can be built.

terms.plain_definition: Changes that suggest someone may be in crisis now, like talking about being a burden, giving things away, withdrawing, or sudden calm after deep despair.
terms.everyday_example: A friend who has been very low suddenly seems at peace and starts saying goodbye-like things.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Not everyone shows warning signs. If you're worried, ask directly and help them connect to support.

terms.plain_definition: A time when someone's distress is so severe they can't stay safe or cope, and need help right away.
terms.everyday_example: Being unable to stop thinking about ending your life, or losing touch with reality.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A crisis is a reason to reach out immediately, by calling a crisis line or emergency services. It is not a sign of weakness.

terms.plain_definition: 'Acute' means sudden and short-term. 'Chronic' means long-lasting or ongoing. 'Episodic' means it comes and goes.
terms.everyday_example: A panic attack is acute; persistent depressive disorder is chronic; bipolar disorder is episodic.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Chronic' doesn't mean 'hopeless'. Many chronic conditions are well managed.

terms.plain_definition: A period of time when symptoms are present, with a clear start and, usually, an end.
terms.everyday_example: A depressive episode that lasts three months, followed by a year of feeling well.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Having one episode doesn't guarantee another, though it does raise the chance, which is why ongoing support matters.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: When a condition first starts. Many mental health conditions begin in the teens or early twenties.
terms.everyday_example: Anxiety that started around age 11 and became hard to manage by 16.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Early onset isn't a sentence. It's a reason to get support early, when it helps most.

terms.plain_definition: What a clinician expects to happen over time, based on what's known about the condition and the person.
terms.everyday_example: 'Good prognosis with treatment' means most people in this situation get better.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A prognosis is a prediction about groups of people, not a fixed fate for you.

terms.plain_definition: To do with how the brain grows and develops from early life. Neurodevelopmental conditions, like autism and ADHD, are lifelong differences, not illnesses that start and stop.
terms.everyday_example: A child's brain wires attention differently from birth; it doesn't 'catch' ADHD later.
terms.common_misunderstanding: These are differences in how a brain works, not damage. Many come with real strengths.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: The everyday skills needed to live independently: communication, self-care, managing money, getting around, relationships.
terms.everyday_example: Being able to cook a meal, use a bus, and know when to ask for help.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Intellectual disability is defined by adaptive functioning as well as test scores. A number alone doesn't describe a person.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: In the UK, 'learning disability' means an intellectual disability affecting overall understanding. 'Learning difficulty' (like dyslexia) affects specific skills. In the US, 'learning disability' means the specific kind. The words clash across countries.
terms.everyday_example: A UK leaflet about 'learning disability' is about something different from a US one.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Check which meaning is in use before assuming. Both deserve respect and support.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: The body's 24-hour internal clock that controls sleep, wakefulness, hormones, and temperature.
terms.everyday_example: Teenagers' clocks naturally run later, which is why early school starts are so hard.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A late body clock isn't laziness. It's biology, and it can be shifted gradually with light and routine.

terms.plain_definition: Sudden muscle weakness triggered by strong emotion, like laughing or surprise, while fully awake. A sign of narcolepsy type 1.
terms.everyday_example: Knees buckling in the middle of a joke, then recovering within seconds.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not fainting or a seizure. People with cataplexy are awake and aware.

terms.plain_definition: Waking up or falling asleep and being unable to move or speak for a few seconds to minutes, sometimes with frightening sensations. Common and harmless.
terms.everyday_example: Opening your eyes, unable to move, feeling a presence in the room, then it passes.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's terrifying but not dangerous, and it's not a sign of mental illness. Lack of sleep and stress make it more likely.

terms.plain_definition: Episodes of screaming or thrashing during deep sleep, usually in children, with no memory of them in the morning. Different from nightmares.
terms.everyday_example: A six-year-old sits up screaming, eyes open, not responding, then settles and remembers nothing.
terms.common_misunderstanding: The child isn't awake and isn't in danger. Most grow out of it.

terms.plain_definition: An umbrella word for serious, ongoing decline in memory and thinking that affects daily life. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause. DSM-5-TR calls it 'major neurocognitive disorder'.
terms.everyday_example: Getting lost on a route driven for 30 years, and not just once.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Dementia isn't normal ageing, and forgetting names occasionally isn't dementia.

sources.title: What Is Dementia? Symptoms, Types, and Diagnosis

terms.plain_definition: Thinking or memory changes that are noticeable and more than expected for age, but don't yet stop a person managing daily life.
terms.everyday_example: Needing lists for things you used to remember easily, but still running your own household.
terms.common_misunderstanding: MCI doesn't always progress to dementia. Some people stay stable or improve.

sources.title: What Is Dementia? Symptoms, Types, and Diagnosis

terms.plain_definition: Increased confusion, restlessness, or agitation in the late afternoon and evening in some people with dementia.
terms.everyday_example: Grandad is calm all morning and becomes anxious and wants to 'go home' every day around 5 p.m.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's a known pattern, not the person being difficult. Light, routine, and calm surroundings can help.

sources.title: What Is Dementia? Symptoms, Types, and Diagnosis

terms.plain_definition: Filling memory gaps with invented details, without meaning to lie. The person believes what they're saying.
terms.everyday_example: Describing a visit from a relative that never happened, in convincing detail.
terms.common_misunderstanding: This isn't lying. It's the brain patching holes. Correcting harshly causes distress for no gain.

terms.plain_definition: Difficulty with language: finding words, speaking, understanding, reading, or writing, because of a change in the brain.
terms.everyday_example: Knowing exactly what you mean and the word simply not coming.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Aphasia affects language, not intelligence.

sources.title: What Is Dementia? Symptoms, Types, and Diagnosis

terms.plain_definition: A lasting pattern in how someone tends to think, feel, and act, like being outgoing or cautious. Traits are normal; everyone has them.
terms.everyday_example: Being the friend who always plans ahead.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A trait only becomes part of a 'disorder' when it's extreme, rigid, and causes lasting harm or distress.

terms.plain_definition: Seeing people or situations as all good or all bad, with sudden flips between the two. Common in borderline personality disorder, and in everyone under stress.
terms.everyday_example: A friend is perfect on Monday and, after a cancelled plan, a traitor on Tuesday.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Splitting is a defence against overwhelming feelings, not manipulation. Therapy helps build the 'grey'.

terms.plain_definition: Not having a steady sense of who you are: values, goals, and even personality can feel like they change depending on who you're with.
terms.everyday_example: Feeling like a different person with each friend group and not knowing which is 'really you'.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Everyone explores identity, especially in the teens. It's a concern when it's severe, painful, and ongoing into adulthood.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: Acting quickly on urges without thinking through the consequences.
terms.everyday_example: Buying a motorbike on a whim, or blurting something out and instantly regretting it.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Impulsivity is a brain-based tendency seen in ADHD, bipolar disorder, and BPD. It can be worked with, not just blamed.

terms.plain_definition: The emotional bond between a child and their caregivers, which shapes how safe they feel in relationships later. 'Attachment styles' (secure, anxious, avoidant, disorganized) describe common patterns.
terms.everyday_example: Feeling panicky when a partner doesn't text back might be an anxious attachment pattern.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Online quizzes oversimplify attachment. Styles aren't fixed labels; they can shift with safe relationships and therapy.

terms.plain_definition: A person's inner sense of their own gender. 'Transgender' means it differs from the sex assigned at birth; 'cisgender' means it matches; 'nonbinary' means it isn't simply male or female.
terms.everyday_example: Knowing from a young age that the gender everyone assumes doesn't fit.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Being transgender is not a mental illness. 'Gender dysphoria' in DSM-5-TR names the distress some trans people feel, not their identity.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: The ICD-11 term (used by the World Health Organization) for a mismatch between a person's gender and their assigned sex. ICD-11 placed it outside the mental-disorders chapter.
terms.everyday_example: A clinic letter in some countries may say 'gender incongruence' instead of 'gender dysphoria'.
terms.common_misunderstanding: The two manuals use different words because they see the issue differently. Neither word says a trans person is 'disordered'.

sources.title: ICD-11 for Mortality and Morbidity Statistics

terms.plain_definition: A paraphilia is an unusual sexual interest. It becomes a paraphilic disorder only when it causes the person serious distress, or involves harm or risk to others. Most unusual interests are not disorders.
terms.everyday_example: A consenting adult kink is not a disorder. An interest that drives someone to harm others is.
terms.common_misunderstanding: DSM-5 made this distinction clearly to stop labelling people as ill for private, consensual interests.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: The natural response to losing someone or something important. It comes in waves and has no set timetable. 'Bereavement' is the loss itself; 'mourning' is how we express grief.
terms.everyday_example: Months after a parent's death, a song in a shop brings sudden tears, then the day goes on.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Grief is not a disorder and doesn't need 'fixing'. Only a small number of people develop prolonged grief that needs extra help.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)
A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Grieving before a loss happens, such as when someone you love has a terminal illness or dementia.
terms.everyday_example: Mourning your mum's old self while she's still alive but no longer knows you.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's real grief, and it doesn't make the eventual loss hurt less.

terms.plain_definition: Grief that others don't recognize or allow, like for an ex-partner, a pet, a miscarriage, or someone who died by suicide or overdose.
terms.everyday_example: Being told 'it was only a dog' when you're devastated.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Your grief is valid even when society doesn't give it a card or a day off.

terms.plain_definition: An event, or a series of events, that overwhelms a person's ability to cope and leaves lasting effects. It's about the impact on the person, not just the size of the event.
terms.everyday_example: A car crash, abuse, a sudden death, or years of being bullied can all be traumatic.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Not everyone who goes through something awful develops PTSD. And 'trauma' online is often used for ordinary upsets; the clinical meaning is more specific.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Trauma that is repeated or long-lasting, often in childhood, like ongoing abuse or neglect. 'Complex PTSD' is an ICD-11 diagnosis for its effects: PTSD plus difficulty with emotions, self-worth, and relationships.
terms.everyday_example: Growing up never knowing if a parent would be kind or cruel, and as an adult struggling with trust and shame.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Complex PTSD is not in DSM-5-TR, but the experiences are real and treatable. In the US, it's usually diagnosed as PTSD with extra features.

sources.title: ICD-11 for Mortality and Morbidity Statistics
A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Stressful or traumatic events before age 18, like abuse, neglect, or living with addiction or violence at home. More ACEs raise the risk of later health problems, but don't decide them.
terms.everyday_example: A child who grows up with a parent in prison and another with untreated depression has two ACEs.
terms.common_misunderstanding: An ACE score is not a destiny. Supportive relationships are powerful protection.

terms.plain_definition: The deep distress of having done, witnessed, or failed to stop something that goes against your core values. Common in veterans and healthcare workers.
terms.everyday_example: A nurse haunted by patients she couldn't help during a crisis, feeling she failed them.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not the same as PTSD, though they can overlap. Shame and guilt are central, and they can be worked through.

terms.plain_definition: The effects of repeatedly hearing about or witnessing others' trauma, common in carers, therapists, first responders, and moderators.
terms.everyday_example: A social worker who starts having nightmares about her clients' stories.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's an occupational hazard, not a weakness, and good supervision and rest protect against it.

terms.plain_definition: An approach where services assume anyone might have a trauma history and act to avoid re-traumatizing: offering choice, explaining what will happen, and not forcing.
terms.everyday_example: A dentist asking before reclining the chair and explaining each step.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Being trauma-informed doesn't mean avoiding all hard topics. It means doing them safely, with consent.

terms.plain_definition: Words used by many people with dissociative identity disorder (DID). 'Alters' or 'parts' are the distinct identity states; 'system' is the whole group sharing one body.
terms.everyday_example: 'Our system has five alters; today the one at the front is Sam.'
terms.common_misunderstanding: Alters aren't 'imaginary friends' or acting. They are how the mind organized itself to survive early trauma.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: The first time someone experiences psychosis. Special 'early intervention' teams exist in many countries because fast, well-rounded help in the first years gives the best outcomes.
terms.everyday_example: A 19-year-old referred to an early intervention team within days of first hearing voices.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A first episode doesn't mean a lifetime of illness. Many people have one episode and recover fully.

terms.plain_definition: Living a meaningful, hopeful life, with or without ongoing symptoms. In the recovery model, the person defines what recovery means, not a checklist.
terms.everyday_example: Someone who still hears voices sometimes, holds a job, has friends, and considers themselves recovered.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Recovery isn't only 'no symptoms'. It's about a life worth living, on your own terms.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Practical ways to reduce the damage from substance use for people who are not ready or able to stop, such as needle programmes and naloxone. It meets people where they are.
terms.everyday_example: A service that gives out clean supplies and overdose kits without requiring abstinence.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Harm reduction doesn't 'enable' use. The evidence shows it saves lives and brings more people into treatment.

terms.plain_definition: Deep exhaustion, cynicism, and feeling useless after long-term stress, usually from work or caring. The World Health Organization lists it as a work-related problem, not an illness.
terms.everyday_example: Dreading Monday by Saturday, doing the bare minimum, and feeling nothing you do matters.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Burnout isn't a diagnosis, but it's real, and it can slide into depression if ignored. Rest alone often isn't enough; something about the load has to change.

sources.title: Burn-out an 'occupational phenomenon': International Classification of Diseases
A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: A sudden surge of intense fear with strong body symptoms: pounding heart, shaking, breathlessness, dizziness, feeling unreal, fearing you're dying or losing control. It peaks within minutes.
terms.everyday_example: In a supermarket queue your heart races, the walls close in, and you're sure something terrible is happening.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A panic attack feels dangerous but isn't. Having one doesn't mean you have panic disorder; that's when attacks keep coming and you start living in fear of the next.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)

terms.plain_definition: An intense, visible reaction to being overwhelmed, often from too much sensory input, change, or demand. Can look like crying, shouting, or lashing out. Common in autistic people and in ADHD.
terms.everyday_example: After a loud day at school, a child screams and throws things at home. The tank is empty.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A meltdown is not a tantrum. It isn't a choice or a strategy to get something; it's an overflow.

terms.plain_definition: The quiet version of a meltdown: going silent, still, and unresponsive when overwhelmed. The person may not be able to speak or move much for a while.
terms.everyday_example: At a party, you stop being able to talk and just want to sit in a dark room.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A shutdown can look like sulking or rudeness. It's a nervous system that has hit its limit.

terms.plain_definition: Hiding natural traits to fit in: forcing eye contact, scripting conversations, suppressing stims, copying others. Common in autistic people, especially women and girls, and in ADHD.
terms.everyday_example: Rehearsing small talk, performing 'normal' all day, then collapsing at home.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Masking is often praised as 'coping well', but it's exhausting and is linked to burnout and depression.

terms.plain_definition: Long-lasting exhaustion, loss of skills, and reduced tolerance for sensory input after prolonged masking or overload. Can last months.
terms.everyday_example: An adult who used to manage work and friendships finds they can't cook or answer messages for weeks.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not depression, though they can overlap, and it doesn't respond to 'pushing through'. Reducing demands is the treatment.

terms.plain_definition: Sudden, unwanted thoughts or pictures that pop into your head and feel upsetting or 'not like you'. Almost everyone has them sometimes.
terms.everyday_example: Standing on a balcony and suddenly picturing dropping your phone, or worse, and feeling scared by the thought.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Having a scary thought does not mean you want it to happen. The distress you feel proves it goes against your values.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Compulsively scrolling through bad news or upsetting content for long stretches, even though it makes you feel worse.
terms.everyday_example: It's 1 a.m. and you've been reading about disasters for two hours, feeling sick but unable to stop.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It isn't a diagnosis, but it feeds anxiety and ruins sleep. Setting limits is a real act of self-care.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Going over the same worries or painful thoughts again and again without getting anywhere. It feels like problem-solving but isn't.
terms.everyday_example: Replaying an awkward comment from three days ago for the hundredth time.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Rumination isn't the same as reflecting. Reflecting leads somewhere; rumination loops. Therapy can teach how to step out of the loop.

terms.plain_definition: Having feelings that come on fast, hit hard, and are tough to bring back down. The emotion is often fair; the size and speed are the problem.
terms.everyday_example: A small disappointment leads to hours of crying or rage, then exhaustion.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not immaturity or drama. Skills like those in DBT are built for this and work.

terms.plain_definition: Putting everyone else's needs first, finding it very hard to say no, and feeling anxious about disappointing anyone. Often learned as a way to stay safe.
terms.everyday_example: Agreeing to a shift you can't do, then lying awake stressing about it.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not a diagnosis or a 'nice person' trait. It's often a survival pattern that therapy can gently unpick.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Feeling like a fraud who will be 'found out', despite real achievements. Very common, especially in new roles and in people from under-represented groups.
terms.everyday_example: Getting a promotion and being sure it was a mistake.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Not a diagnosis. It's a thinking pattern, and talking about it usually reveals most people around you feel it too.

terms.plain_definition: A strong attachment to someone who hurts you, built by cycles of cruelty and kindness. It explains why leaving an abusive relationship can feel impossible.
terms.everyday_example: Feeling intense love for a partner right after they've frightened you, because they apologized.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A trauma bond isn't love or weakness. It's a predictable response to intermittent abuse, and support helps people break it.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Making someone doubt their own memory or sanity by repeatedly denying things that happened. It's a form of emotional abuse.
terms.everyday_example: 'I never said that. You're imagining things again,' about something you clearly remember.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Online it's often used for any disagreement. Real gaslighting is a deliberate, repeated pattern that makes a person question reality.

terms.plain_definition: A popular phrase for depression in someone who keeps working, studying, and showing up while feeling awful inside. Often what clinicians call persistent depressive disorder.
terms.everyday_example: Top grades, a job, a social life, and crying in the shower every morning.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'High-functioning' isn't a diagnosis and can be a trap: looking fine makes it harder to get help. The pain counts even when the performance is good.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Depression that arrives with the darker months and lifts in spring. In DSM-5-TR it's depression 'with seasonal pattern'.
terms.everyday_example: Every November the energy drains and nothing seems worth doing until the clocks change.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Winter blues' is mild and common. Seasonal depression is heavier and treatable, including with light therapy and talking therapy.

terms.plain_definition: A way of explaining limited energy, from a 2003 essay by Christine Miserandino. Each 'spoon' is a unit of energy; illness or disability means fewer spoons per day, so every task costs.
terms.everyday_example: 'I can't come tonight, I used my spoons on the doctor's appointment.'
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's a metaphor, not a medical model, and it belongs to the chronic illness and disability community. Use it with respect.

terms.plain_definition: Feeling criticism or rejection, real or imagined, as intense emotional pain. 'RSD' is a popular term in the ADHD community; it's not an official diagnosis.
terms.everyday_example: A friend says 'maybe next time' and you spiral into feeling unlovable for the rest of the day.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Not an official term, but the experience is real and common in ADHD and social anxiety. Naming it helps people feel less alone.

terms.plain_definition: The body's response to pressure. Short bursts are normal and even useful. Long-lasting ('chronic') stress with no relief wears down mind and body.
terms.everyday_example: Weeks of deadlines, poor sleep, and tight shoulders that never loosen.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Stress is not a mental illness, but ongoing stress raises the risk of one. Taking it seriously early is prevention.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health
Mental Health and Behavior
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus, US National Library of Medicine

terms.plain_definition: An everyday phrase, not a diagnosis, for a time when stress becomes so overwhelming that a person can't function. Underneath is usually depression, anxiety, or burnout.
terms.everyday_example: 'Mum had a breakdown after the divorce' might mean a severe depressive episode.
terms.common_misunderstanding: The phrase is vague but the experience is real. Clinicians will look for the specific condition so it can be treated.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Having more demands, feelings, or sensations than you can process at once, so everything seems impossible.
terms.everyday_example: Looking at a to-do list of ten small things and being unable to start any of them.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Overwhelm is a state, not a trait. Reducing input and picking one tiny next step is often the way out.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Online, 'triggered' often means 'annoyed' or 'offended'. The clinical meaning is a sudden, overwhelming reaction linked to trauma or a condition.
terms.everyday_example: Someone says they're 'triggered' by a bad film review; a trauma survivor is triggered by a smell that brings a flashback.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Using 'triggered' as a joke makes it harder for people with real triggers to be taken seriously.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: A popular word for relationships, workplaces, or behaviours that consistently harm someone's wellbeing. Not a clinical term.
terms.everyday_example: A friendship where you always leave feeling worse about yourself.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Toxic' describes a pattern's effect on you; it isn't a diagnosis of the other person. Both can be true: the pattern is harmful and the person isn't a monster.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Online, 'narcissist' is thrown at anyone selfish or difficult. Narcissistic personality disorder is a specific, uncommon diagnosis that only a clinician can make.
terms.everyday_example: Calling an ex 'a narcissist' after a bad breakup.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Self-centred behaviour isn't a disorder. Armchair diagnosing others, however satisfying, usually doesn't help you heal and can be unfair to people with the actual condition.

terms.plain_definition: Overwhelming someone with affection, gifts, and attention very early in a relationship, often followed by control or withdrawal. A warning sign of abusive patterns.
terms.everyday_example: Declarations of 'soulmates' and constant gifts in week one, then anger if you want a night alone.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Intense early romance isn't always love bombing. The red flag is when the intensity is used to control you.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Limits you set on what you will and won't accept, to protect your wellbeing. Healthy boundaries are about your own actions, not controlling others.
terms.everyday_example: 'I'm not available to talk about this after 9 p.m.'
terms.common_misunderstanding: A boundary isn't a punishment or an ultimatum. It's information about what you need.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Anything you do on purpose to look after your physical, mental, or emotional health. Often unglamorous: sleep, meals, bills, saying no, seeing the doctor.
terms.everyday_example: Going to bed at ten instead of scrolling, or booking the appointment you've put off.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Self-care is not bubble baths and shopping, and it's not a replacement for treatment. It's the daily maintenance that makes treatment work better.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Simple techniques that bring your attention back to the present when anxiety, flashbacks, or dissociation take over, often through the senses.
terms.everyday_example: Naming five things you can see, four you can hear, three you can touch.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Grounding doesn't 'cure' anything. It's a tool for getting through a hard moment safely.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Working alongside another person, in the room or on video, to make it easier to start and finish tasks. Popular in the ADHD community.
terms.everyday_example: Opening a video call with a friend and both doing your taxes in silence.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not cheating or dependence. External structure is a legitimate tool for a brain that struggles with starting.

terms.plain_definition: Difficulty sensing how much time has passed or how long things take, common in ADHD.
terms.everyday_example: Being sure you have 'loads of time' and then being 40 minutes late, again.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not rudeness or not caring. Timers, alarms, and visual clocks help because the internal clock doesn't.

terms.plain_definition: Becoming so absorbed in something interesting that time, hunger, and the outside world disappear. Common in ADHD and autism.
terms.everyday_example: Starting a project at 8 p.m. and looking up at 3 a.m. with a full bladder and an empty stomach.
terms.common_misunderstanding: If someone with ADHD can hyperfocus on games, it doesn't mean they're 'choosing' not to focus on homework. Interest drives attention, not willpower.

terms.plain_definition: A deep, passionate, long-lasting interest in a topic, common in autistic people. 'Infodumping' is joyfully sharing everything you know about it.
terms.everyday_example: Knowing every detail about trains, or fungi, or one historical period, and lighting up when asked.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Special interests aren't 'obsessions' to be cured. They're a source of joy, skill, and often careers.

terms.plain_definition: When sounds, lights, smells, or crowds all come in at once and the brain can't filter them, leading to distress, meltdown, or shutdown.
terms.everyday_example: A busy shopping centre: music, lights, chatter, and perfume until you have to leave.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not being 'too sensitive'. Noise-cancelling headphones and quiet spaces are reasonable adjustments, not special treatment.

terms.plain_definition: 'Neurodivergent' means having a brain that works differently from what's typical, such as autism, ADHD, dyslexia, or Tourette's. 'Neurotypical' means not. 'Neurodiversity' is the idea that these differences are natural variation.
terms.everyday_example: 'I'm neurodivergent' as a way to explain needing clear instructions without naming a diagnosis.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Neurodivergent isn't a diagnosis, and being neurodivergent doesn't mean something is wrong with you. It also doesn't erase real support needs.

terms.plain_definition: Being diagnosed with autism, ADHD, or similar as an adult, often after years of being misunderstood or diagnosed with something else.
terms.everyday_example: Finding out at 38 that the 'anxiety' and 'laziness' were ADHD all along.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A late diagnosis often brings grief for the past as well as relief. Both are normal.

terms.plain_definition: Identifying with a condition based on your own research, without a professional assessment. Common where assessment is expensive or has long waits.
terms.everyday_example: Recognizing yourself in every ADHD video and deciding that explains your life.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Self-exploration is valuable and can be a first step. But many conditions overlap, and only an assessment can rule things in or out and open doors to treatment and accommodations.

terms.plain_definition: Feeling mentally slow, forgetful, and unable to concentrate. A symptom, not a diagnosis, with many causes: depression, anxiety, poor sleep, illness, medication, menopause.
terms.everyday_example: Reading the same email four times and still not knowing what it says.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Brain fog is real and worth mentioning to a doctor, who will look for the cause.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Drifting off mentally and losing track of what's around you. Mild and common. Online, 'dissociating' is sometimes used for this.
terms.everyday_example: Staring at the wall during a lecture and realizing you missed ten minutes.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Occasional zoning out is normal. Frequent, long, or distressing episodes, or losing time, are worth raising with a professional.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Using 'OCD' to mean tidy or particular. OCD is a serious condition of unwanted thoughts and exhausting rituals, not a preference for neatness.
terms.everyday_example: 'I'm so OCD about my desk.'
terms.common_misunderstanding: People with OCD often have no interest in tidiness; their obsessions are about harm, contamination, or doubt. The joke trivializes real suffering.

terms.plain_definition: Using 'bipolar' to describe moody weather or a changeable person. Bipolar disorder involves episodes of mania and depression lasting days to months, not moment-to-moment mood swings.
terms.everyday_example: 'The weather's so bipolar today.'
terms.common_misunderstanding: Casual use spreads the myth that bipolar disorder is just moodiness, which makes it harder for people to be taken seriously.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Words like 'crazy', 'psycho', 'addict', 'schizo', or 'committed suicide' attach shame to illness. This project uses 'person with…' or community-preferred identity-first terms, and 'died by suicide'.
terms.everyday_example: 'He's a psycho' versus 'he's unwell and needs help'.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Changing words isn't being 'soft'. Research shows language affects whether people seek help and how they're treated.

terms.plain_definition: Everyone has mental health, which can be good or poor, like physical health. A mental illness (or disorder) is a diagnosable condition. You can have a diagnosis and good mental health, or no diagnosis and poor mental health.
terms.everyday_example: A person with well-managed bipolar disorder may have better mental health than a stressed, sleepless colleague with no diagnosis.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Mental health' is not a polite word for 'mental illness'. They're different things.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health
Mental Health and Behavior
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus, US National Library of Medicine

terms.plain_definition: A general sense of feeling good and functioning well. 'Flourishing' is high wellbeing; 'languishing' is the flat, 'meh' middle state that isn't illness but isn't thriving.
terms.everyday_example: Not depressed, but not excited about anything either; just going through the motions.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Languishing isn't a diagnosis, but it's a reasonable reason to make changes or talk to someone before things slide.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: The ability to recover from hard times. It's built by support, skills, and circumstances, not just by personal grit.
terms.everyday_example: Getting through a bereavement with the help of friends, routine, and time.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Telling someone to 'be more resilient' ignores that resilience comes largely from having support. It isn't a character test.

terms.plain_definition: The things you do to get through stress or difficult feelings. Some help long-term (talking, exercise, problem-solving); some help now but hurt later (drinking, avoiding).
terms.everyday_example: Going for a walk when angry instead of sending the text.
terms.common_misunderstanding: There are no 'bad' people, only coping strategies that cost too much. Therapy often means swapping costly ones for cheaper ones.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: The people and services you can lean on: friends, family, peers, professionals, groups, helplines.
terms.everyday_example: A list on your fridge of three people to call and one helpline number.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A support system doesn't have to be big. One or two safe people and a crisis line count.

terms.plain_definition: A dismissive phrase used to tell someone their symptoms aren't real. Mental health conditions are in the brain, which is in the head, and they're real.
terms.everyday_example: A doctor saying it about fatigue and pain that later turns out to be depression plus a thyroid problem.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Symptoms being linked to the mind doesn't make them less real or less treatable.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: The idea that someone can choose to stop being depressed or anxious. They can't, any more than someone can choose to stop having asthma.
terms.everyday_example: 'Have you tried just not worrying?'
terms.common_misunderstanding: Effort and choices do matter in recovery, but they work alongside treatment and support, not instead of them.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: A label often put on self-harm, suicidal talk, or dramatic distress. If someone needs attention that badly, that is itself a sign they need help.
terms.everyday_example: A teenager's self-harm dismissed as 'just for attention'.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Most people who self-harm hide it. And seeking connection when in pain is healthy, not manipulative.

terms.plain_definition: A judgement often attached to people with borderline personality disorder or in crisis. Most 'manipulative' behaviour is a desperate attempt to get needs met with the only tools available.
terms.everyday_example: Calling someone manipulative for threatening self-harm when a partner wants to leave.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Seeing the need behind the behaviour helps more than the label. This is a known source of stigma, including in healthcare.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Often what depression, ADHD, executive dysfunction, or chronic illness looks like from outside.
terms.everyday_example: A student who can't get out of bed called lazy, when they haven't slept properly in weeks.
terms.common_misunderstanding: In clinical experience, 'laziness' is almost always something else: low energy, fear, overwhelm, or a brain that can't start.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Anxiety, dread, and shame the day after drinking, as the calming effect of alcohol wears off and the brain rebounds.
terms.everyday_example: Waking up at 5 a.m. after a party, heart racing, convinced you said something terrible.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's a real chemical effect, and if it's frequent it's a sign to look at both the drinking and the anxiety.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Staying up late on purpose to claim some free time after a day that felt controlled by others, even though you'll pay for it tomorrow.
terms.everyday_example: Scrolling until 2 a.m. because it's the only part of the day that's yours.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not a disorder, but it feeds insomnia and burnout. The fix is usually about the day, not the night.

terms.plain_definition: The painful feeling of not having the connection you need. You can be lonely in a crowd, and alone without being lonely. Long-term loneliness harms health.
terms.everyday_example: Living in a busy city and going a week without a real conversation.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Loneliness isn't a personal failing. It's a signal, like hunger, and many groups exist just to help people connect.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: A popular metaphor for how much social energy you have before you need to recharge alone. Introverts and neurodivergent people often have a smaller or faster-draining battery.
terms.everyday_example: Loving a party for two hours and needing a day of quiet after.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Needing alone time isn't social anxiety or rudeness. It's a normal difference in how people recharge.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Shyness and introversion are normal personality traits. Social anxiety disorder is intense fear of being judged that leads to avoiding things you want or need to do.
terms.everyday_example: An introvert happily skips the party. Someone with social anxiety wants to go, can't, and hates themselves for it.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Not every quiet person has a disorder, and not every outgoing person is free of one.

terms.plain_definition: Setting impossibly high standards and feeling like a failure when they aren't met. It fuels anxiety, procrastination, eating disorders, and burnout.
terms.everyday_example: Rewriting an email seven times, then not sending it because it isn't 'right'.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Perfectionism isn't 'high standards'. High standards let you finish; perfectionism stops you.

terms.plain_definition: Putting off tasks even though you know it will cost you. Usually driven by anxiety, overwhelm, or executive function struggles, not laziness.
terms.everyday_example: The essay is due tomorrow; you've cleaned the whole flat instead.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Understanding why you avoid a task helps far more than self-criticism.

terms.plain_definition: The harsh voice in your head that judges everything you do. Everyone has one; in depression and anxiety it gets much louder.
terms.everyday_example: 'You're useless, everyone can see it,' after a small mistake.
terms.common_misunderstanding: The inner critic sounds like truth but is a habit of thought, often learned from others. Therapy can turn down its volume.

terms.plain_definition: Seeing things in extremes: total success or complete failure, perfect or worthless, with no middle.
terms.everyday_example: Missing one workout and deciding the whole plan is ruined.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A common thinking trap in depression, anxiety, eating disorders, and BPD. Learning to find the grey is a core therapy skill.

terms.plain_definition: A popular term for a relationship pattern where one person's sense of worth depends on caring for or rescuing another, often someone with addiction. Not a diagnosis.
terms.everyday_example: Covering for a partner's drinking for years while your own life shrinks.
terms.common_misunderstanding: The idea came from family recovery groups and can be useful, but it can also blame people for loving someone who is unwell. Use it gently.
