terms.plain_definition: Family relationships with no healthy boundaries, where a child is expected to meet a parent's emotional needs ('parentification') or where individuality isn't allowed.
terms.everyday_example: A ten-year-old who is their mother's main confidant and comforter.
terms.common_misunderstanding: These patterns are often invisible from inside and are not the child's fault. Therapy can help adults untangle them.

terms.plain_definition: Growing up without enough emotional attention, comfort, or interest, even if physical needs were met. Its effects are often felt as adults who don't know what they feel or need.
terms.everyday_example: Parents who paid for everything but never asked how you were.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Neglect is about what didn't happen, so people often don't recognize it as harm. It is, and it's a recognized form of maltreatment.

terms.plain_definition: A therapy idea: the part of you that still carries childhood feelings and needs. 'Reparenting' means giving yourself now the care you missed then.
terms.everyday_example: Talking kindly to yourself the way you'd talk to a scared seven-year-old.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's a metaphor used in several therapies, not a literal second person. Some people find it powerful; others don't, and that's fine.

terms.plain_definition: The body's automatic responses to threat: fight back, run, go still, or appease. 'Fawn' is a popular addition for people-pleasing under threat.
terms.everyday_example: Freezing and going quiet during an argument instead of responding.
terms.common_misunderstanding: These responses are automatic, not chosen. Blaming yourself for freezing during something frightening is unfair; your body did what it's built to do.

terms.plain_definition: A popular therapy model: the zone where you can handle feelings and think clearly. Above it is panic or rage; below it is numbness or shutdown. Trauma narrows the window; therapy widens it.
terms.everyday_example: Noticing you're 'above the window' and using breathing to come back down.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's a teaching model, not a measurement. Useful for understanding why you react so strongly some days.

terms.plain_definition: A popular, non-clinical label for people who process things deeply and are easily overstimulated. It overlaps with traits seen in autism, ADHD, and anxiety.
terms.everyday_example: Crying at adverts, needing quiet after busy days, noticing every shift in someone's mood.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'HSP' isn't a diagnosis and isn't in any manual. For some it's a helpful identity; for others it hides a condition that could be supported.

terms.plain_definition: A popular phrase for going through the motions of life while feeling numb, stuck, and unable to do more than the basics. Not a diagnosis; often depression, burnout, or trauma underneath.
terms.everyday_example: Going to work, coming home, lying on the floor, repeat, for months.
terms.common_misunderstanding: The phrase names something real, but naming it isn't treatment. If this describes you, it's worth talking to someone.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Spending the day in bed scrolling, snacking, and resting, framed online as self-care. Sometimes it is; sometimes it's depression in disguise.
terms.everyday_example: A Sunday in bed to recover from a hard week versus a third week of not being able to get up.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Rest is good. Being unable to get up, day after day, is a symptom worth attention, not a lifestyle.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: A popular term for longing for physical contact after a long time without it. Humans need safe touch; going without affects mood.
terms.everyday_example: Realizing after months alone that a hug from a friend made you tearful.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Not a diagnosis, but a real need. Safe ways to meet it include hugs with trusted people, pets, and massage.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: A Japanese word for severe social withdrawal: staying at home and avoiding almost all contact for six months or more. Now described worldwide.
terms.everyday_example: A young adult who hasn't left their room except at night for over a year.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not laziness or 'just being a gamer'. Underneath is often anxiety, depression, or shame, and gentle, patient support helps.

sources.title: ICD-11 for Mortality and Morbidity Statistics

terms.plain_definition: A popular term for an unhealthy obsession with 'clean' or 'pure' eating that takes over life and harms health. Not an official diagnosis; it's usually seen as a form of eating disorder.
terms.everyday_example: Cutting out more and more foods until eating with friends becomes impossible.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Caring about nutrition is fine. It's a problem when rules replace flexibility and fear replaces enjoyment.

terms.plain_definition: The set of beliefs that thinness equals health and worth, and that food is 'good' or 'bad'. It's everywhere and it feeds eating disorders.
terms.everyday_example: 'Earning' a dessert through exercise, or praising someone for weight loss without knowing why they lost it.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Commenting on bodies and food, even kindly, can harm. This project never gives weights, calories, or 'before and after' detail.

terms.plain_definition: Online, 'addicted' means 'really like'. Clinically, a substance use disorder means losing control and continuing despite harm. 'Addictive personality' is not a real thing.
terms.everyday_example: 'I'm addicted to this show' versus being unable to stop drinking despite losing a job.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Loose use of 'addict' as a noun is stigmatizing. Say 'a person with a substance use disorder' or 'in recovery'.

sources.title: Drugs, Brains, and Behavior: The Science of Addiction

terms.plain_definition: Choosing to drink less or not at all for wellbeing, without necessarily having a drinking problem.
terms.everyday_example: Doing a dry month and noticing better sleep and mood.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's fine to cut down without a diagnosis. If stopping feels impossible or causes withdrawal, that's a sign to talk to a doctor.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Crying easily, often, or for no clear reason. Common in depression, grief, perinatal mood changes, and burnout. Also a side effect of some situations like exhaustion.
terms.everyday_example: Bursting into tears at the checkout and not knowing why.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Crying isn't weakness or 'being dramatic'. Frequent unexplained crying is a symptom worth mentioning.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Sudden, intense anger in parents, often from exhaustion, overload, and no support. Popular term; may be a sign of perinatal depression or anxiety.
terms.everyday_example: Screaming at a toddler over spilled milk, then crying with guilt.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It doesn't make someone a bad parent. It's often a symptom of a treatable condition and a sign of needing more help.

terms.plain_definition: Popular phrases for the ongoing process of recovering from trauma or mental health difficulties. Can be empowering, or can create pressure to be constantly 'working on yourself'.
terms.everyday_example: Months of therapy, journaling, and tough conversations, with setbacks along the way.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Healing isn't a straight line and doesn't need to be a full-time job. Rest is part of it.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Online, therapy words like 'boundaries', 'gaslighting', 'trauma', and 'narcissist' get stretched far beyond their meaning. This glossary gives the real meaning and the popular one side by side.
terms.everyday_example: A disagreement called 'gaslighting', a preference called a 'boundary', a bad day called 'trauma'.
terms.common_misunderstanding: The words spread because people are reaching for ways to describe pain. That's good. Using them accurately keeps them useful.

terms.plain_definition: Working with a trained professional to understand and change thoughts, feelings, and behaviours. There are many types; the relationship with the therapist matters as much as the method.
terms.everyday_example: Weekly sessions for a few months to work through anxiety that's been holding you back.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Therapy isn't just 'talking about your childhood' or only for crises. Most therapies are practical and time-limited.

terms.plain_definition: A practical, structured therapy that looks at how thoughts, feelings, and actions feed each other, and teaches skills to change unhelpful patterns. One of the most studied treatments for anxiety and depression.
terms.everyday_example: Keeping a thought record, then testing 'everyone will laugh at me' by actually speaking up in a meeting.
terms.common_misunderstanding: CBT isn't 'just think positive'. It's about thinking accurately and acting differently, and it involves homework.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: A skills-based therapy built for intense emotions and self-harm, originally for borderline personality disorder. It teaches mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, and relationship skills, usually in group plus individual sessions.
terms.everyday_example: Learning to 'ride the wave' of an urge for 20 minutes instead of acting on it.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Dialectical' means holding two truths: accepting yourself as you are and working to change. It's not either/or.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: A therapy that teaches you to make room for difficult thoughts and feelings instead of fighting them, and to act on what matters to you anyway.
terms.everyday_example: Noticing 'I'm having the thought that I'll fail' and going to the interview regardless.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Acceptance isn't giving up. It's dropping the exhausting struggle so you have energy for your life.

terms.plain_definition: A trauma therapy where you briefly focus on a memory while following side-to-side eye movements or taps. It helps the brain file the memory so it stops feeling like it's happening now.
terms.everyday_example: After several sessions, the car crash memory is still there but no longer makes your heart race.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It can sound strange, but EMDR is recommended for PTSD by NICE and the WHO. It isn't hypnosis.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: The main therapy for OCD. You gradually face what triggers obsessions while not doing the compulsion, so the brain learns the anxiety passes on its own.
terms.everyday_example: Touching a door handle and waiting out the urge to wash, starting small and building up.
terms.common_misunderstanding: ERP is hard but not cruel. It's done at your pace, with a therapist, and it's the most effective treatment for OCD.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: Facing feared situations step by step, from easiest to hardest, until the fear fades. Used for phobias, panic, social anxiety, and PTSD.
terms.everyday_example: For a fear of dogs: looking at photos, then watching one through a window, then standing near a calm dog on a lead.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Exposure isn't being thrown in the deep end. Each step is agreed with you, and you stay until the anxiety drops.

terms.plain_definition: Therapies designed for PTSD. Cognitive processing therapy works on the beliefs trauma left behind; prolonged exposure works through the memory and avoided situations; TF-CBT is a version for children and families.
terms.everyday_example: Writing about the event in detail with a therapist until it loses its grip.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Avoiding the memory feels safer, but the trauma-focused approaches are the ones with the strongest evidence.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: A time-limited therapy for depression that focuses on relationships and life changes: grief, conflict, role changes, and isolation.
terms.everyday_example: Working on how a parent's death and a move to a new city combined to trigger depression.
terms.common_misunderstanding: IPT isn't couples therapy. It's individual therapy about your relationships.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: A therapy that explores how past experiences and patterns you may not be aware of shape your feelings and relationships now. Usually longer-term and less structured than CBT.
terms.everyday_example: Noticing you treat every boss like your critical father, and understanding why.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not just lying on a couch for years. Modern psychodynamic therapy has evidence for depression, anxiety, and personality difficulties.

terms.plain_definition: A therapy for borderline personality disorder that strengthens the ability to understand your own and others' minds, especially when emotions run high.
terms.everyday_example: Pausing in an argument to wonder what your friend might be feeling, rather than assuming.
terms.common_misunderstanding: MBT is one of several effective treatments for BPD. The condition is treatable; the old idea that it isn't is wrong.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: A longer-term therapy combining CBT, attachment, and emotion-focused ideas to change deep patterns ('schemas') learned in childhood, like 'I'm unlovable'.
terms.everyday_example: Identifying an 'abandonment schema' and learning to respond to it as an adult rather than a scared child.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Schema therapy is slower than CBT but can reach patterns that short therapies don't.

terms.plain_definition: Therapy with the family as a group, treating problems as patterns between people rather than inside one person. Family-based treatment is a specific version that is first-line for teenagers with anorexia.
terms.everyday_example: Parents, a teen, and a therapist working out how mealtimes can support recovery.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Family therapy isn't about blaming parents. It's about using the family as the main resource for change.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: An enhanced form of CBT built for eating disorders in adults. It addresses the thoughts and behaviours that keep the disorder going, including the over-importance of weight and shape.
terms.everyday_example: Regular eating, then gradually tackling food rules and body-checking habits.
terms.common_misunderstanding: CBT-E is not a diet or a meal plan. It's about freedom from the rules, not more rules.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: A simple, well-evidenced depression treatment: scheduling small activities that bring pleasure or purpose, even when you don't feel like it, because action lifts mood more than waiting for mood to lift action.
terms.everyday_example: Putting 'ten-minute walk' in the diary and doing it on a bad day.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It isn't 'just get busy'. Activities are chosen for meaning and value, and the pace is gentle.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: A behavioural therapy for tics and body-focused habits like hair pulling. You learn to notice the urge and do a competing action instead.
terms.everyday_example: Clenching a fist when the urge to pull hair arrives, until it passes.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It isn't about willpower or 'just stopping'. It's about retraining a reflex with practice.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: The recommended first treatment for long-term insomnia. It reshapes sleep habits, the link between bed and sleep, and worries about sleep. Usually a few sessions, sometimes online.
terms.everyday_example: Getting up when you can't sleep instead of lying awake, and keeping a fixed wake time.
terms.common_misunderstanding: CBT-I works better than sleeping tablets in the long run and has no side effects. It's not just 'sleep hygiene tips'.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: Sitting near a special bright lamp for a set time each morning to treat seasonal depression and some sleep-timing problems.
terms.everyday_example: Half an hour at the lamp while eating breakfast, from October to March.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Any lamp won't do; it needs to be a proper light-therapy device. Check with a doctor first, especially with bipolar disorder or eye problems.

terms.plain_definition: Learning about your condition: what it is, what helps, what to watch for. Knowing what's happening reduces fear and improves outcomes. This project is psychoeducation.
terms.everyday_example: A workshop for families about what bipolar disorder is and how to spot early signs of an episode.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not 'just information'. For bipolar disorder and psychosis, psychoeducation measurably reduces relapse.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: Paying attention to the present moment, on purpose and without judgement. Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) is a course that helps prevent depression coming back.
terms.everyday_example: Noticing your breath and your feet on the floor while a wave of worry passes.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Mindfulness isn't emptying your mind or relaxation. For some people, especially with trauma, it can be hard; a trained teacher helps.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: Therapy with several people and one or two therapists. Hearing others and being heard can be as healing as the content.
terms.everyday_example: A weekly group of eight people working on social anxiety together.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Most people dread it beforehand and find it the most helpful part later. You're never forced to share.

terms.plain_definition: Support from people who have been through similar experiences. Peer support workers are trained and employed for this role in many services.
terms.everyday_example: Talking to someone who also hears voices and has learned to live well with them.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Peer support isn't a cheap substitute for professionals. It offers something different: hope from someone who's been there.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: A regular meeting, in person or online, of people with a shared experience, often run by a charity or by peers. Free or low-cost.
terms.everyday_example: A monthly NAMI, Mind, or Beyond Blue group for people with depression.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Support groups aren't therapy and shouldn't replace it, but many people find them the thing that keeps them going between appointments.

terms.plain_definition: Free peer-run fellowships for recovery from alcohol, drugs, gambling, and more, following twelve steps. Al-Anon and Alateen are for families. Meetings are everywhere and online.
terms.everyday_example: Going to a meeting every day for the first 90 days.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 12-step isn't the only way to recover, and it isn't religious, though it uses spiritual language. Try a few meetings; they differ a lot.

terms.plain_definition: A free, science-based mutual-support programme for addictive behaviours, using CBT and motivational tools instead of the 12 steps.
terms.everyday_example: A weekly meeting working through 'cost-benefit analysis' of drinking.
terms.common_misunderstanding: SMART and 12-step aren't rivals. Some people use both.

terms.plain_definition: A way of talking that helps people find their own reasons to change, instead of being told what to do. Widely used in substance use care.
terms.everyday_example: A clinician asking 'what would be better if you drank less?' rather than lecturing.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It isn't manipulation. It respects that people change when they're ready, and helps them get ready.

terms.plain_definition: Prescribed medicines, such as buprenorphine or methadone, that stop withdrawal and cravings so people can rebuild their lives. The most effective treatment for opioid use disorder.
terms.everyday_example: Daily medication from a clinic plus counselling, holding down a job for the first time in years.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It is not 'swapping one addiction for another'. It's treatment, like insulin for diabetes, and it halves the risk of death.

sources.title: Drugs, Brains, and Behavior: The Science of Addiction

terms.plain_definition: A medicine that reverses an opioid overdose within minutes. In many countries it's available free from pharmacies or harm-reduction services, as a nasal spray or injection.
terms.everyday_example: A friend carries naloxone and uses it when someone stops breathing after taking opioids.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Naloxone is safe and can't be misused. Carrying it doesn't encourage drug use; it prevents deaths.

terms.plain_definition: Planning ahead for the situations, feelings, and early signs that could lead back to symptoms or use, and deciding in advance what to do.
terms.everyday_example: A written list: 'If I stop sleeping for three nights, I call my nurse.'
terms.common_misunderstanding: Planning for relapse isn't expecting failure. It's what makes recovery robust.

sources.title: Drugs, Brains, and Behavior: The Science of Addiction
Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: Supervised withdrawal from alcohol or drugs, sometimes with medication, in hospital or at home with support. It's the first step, not the treatment.
terms.everyday_example: A week in a unit coming off alcohol safely, then starting rehab or community support.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Detox alone rarely leads to lasting recovery. What comes after matters most.

terms.plain_definition: A live-in programme, usually weeks to months, for substance use or eating disorders, with therapy, structure, and support.
terms.everyday_example: Three months in a residential centre followed by outpatient aftercare.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Rehab isn't the only route to recovery, and the 'rock bottom' idea is a myth. Many recover in the community.

terms.plain_definition: Medicines that help lift mood and reduce anxiety by changing brain chemistry over weeks. They treat depression, anxiety disorders, OCD, PTSD, and more. Prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
terms.everyday_example: Starting a tablet and noticing after four to six weeks that mornings feel less heavy.
terms.common_misunderstanding: They aren't 'happy pills' and they aren't addictive, though stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal-like symptoms. They work best alongside therapy.

terms.plain_definition: The most commonly prescribed type of antidepressant. They increase available serotonin, a chemical messenger in the brain. Prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
terms.everyday_example: A GP suggesting an SSRI alongside therapy for panic attacks.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Early side effects (nausea, restlessness) usually fade in a couple of weeks. Benefits take longer. Don't stop without talking to your doctor.

terms.plain_definition: Antidepressants that act on two brain messengers, serotonin and noradrenaline. Used for depression, anxiety, and sometimes pain. Prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
terms.everyday_example: Switching to an SNRI when an SSRI helped mood but not energy.
terms.common_misunderstanding: SNRIs and SSRIs are cousins, not identical. Which works best varies by person.

terms.plain_definition: Medicines that even out the highs and lows of bipolar disorder and help prevent new episodes. Lithium is the oldest and best-studied; some epilepsy medicines are also used. Prescribed and monitored by a doctor, often with blood tests.
terms.everyday_example: Taking lithium daily with blood checks every few months, and staying well for years.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Mood stabilizers don't flatten personality. The goal is steady mood with full feeling.

terms.plain_definition: Medicines that reduce hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking, and that also help in mania and some severe depression. Prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
terms.everyday_example: The voices quietening over a few weeks after starting treatment.
terms.common_misunderstanding: The name is off-putting; 'antipsychotic' doesn't mean you're 'psychotic'. Side effects vary a lot between drugs, so it's worth discussing options.

terms.plain_definition: An antipsychotic given as an injection every few weeks instead of daily tablets, which some people prefer for convenience or to avoid missed doses.
terms.everyday_example: A monthly injection at the clinic, no daily pills to remember.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A depot isn't a punishment or only for people who 'won't take tablets'. Many people choose it.

terms.plain_definition: Fast-acting sedatives used short-term for severe anxiety, panic, alcohol withdrawal, or seizures. They work quickly but can cause dependence, so they're usually limited to a few weeks. Prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
terms.everyday_example: A few days of a sedative during a crisis, then tapering off.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Benzodiazepines are not a long-term anxiety treatment, and stopping suddenly after regular use can be dangerous. Never stop without medical advice.

terms.plain_definition: Heart medicines sometimes prescribed to calm physical anxiety symptoms like shaking and pounding heart, for example before a performance. They don't affect the thoughts. Prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
terms.everyday_example: Taking one before a speech so your hands don't shake.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Beta-blockers aren't a treatment for anxiety disorders overall, just for the body side of specific situations.

terms.plain_definition: The main medicines for ADHD. Despite the name, they help the brain focus and settle by boosting messengers involved in attention. Prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
terms.everyday_example: The constant noise in your head going quiet for the first time, and being able to finish a task.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Stimulant medicines, taken as prescribed, don't create addiction and aren't 'cheating'. Non-stimulant options exist too.

terms.plain_definition: Medicines to help sleep, used short-term or for specific conditions. Melatonin is a hormone used mainly for sleep-timing problems and in some neurodevelopmental conditions. Prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
terms.everyday_example: A short course while going through a crisis, while starting CBT for insomnia.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Sleeping tablets don't fix insomnia long-term and can stop working or cause dependence. CBT-I is the first-line treatment.

terms.plain_definition: Unwanted effects of a medicine. Many fade in weeks; some don't. Always worth reporting, because doses and drugs can be changed.
terms.everyday_example: Feeling sick for the first fortnight on an antidepressant, then it passing.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Side effects aren't a reason to stop on your own. They're a reason to talk to the prescriber.

terms.plain_definition: Reducing a medicine gradually, in steps, so the body can adjust. How slowly depends on the drug and the person. Always planned with the prescriber.
terms.everyday_example: Coming off an antidepressant over several months rather than stopping dead.
terms.common_misunderstanding: This project gives no schedules or doses. Tapering is individual and must be done with a doctor.

terms.plain_definition: A treatment for severe depression, catatonia, or mania that hasn't responded to other treatments. A brief electrical current under anaesthetic triggers a controlled seizure. It's done with consent and modern safeguards.
terms.everyday_example: Someone with life-threatening depression who can't eat or drink improving within weeks.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Film portrayals are decades out of date. Modern ECT is painless and can be life-saving, though memory side effects are real and should be discussed.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: A treatment for depression that hasn't responded to medication. A magnetic coil on the scalp stimulates brain areas involved in mood. No anaesthetic; sessions over several weeks.
terms.everyday_example: Daily 20-minute sessions for six weeks, while carrying on with normal life.
terms.common_misunderstanding: TMS isn't ECT. It's milder, with fewer side effects, and it isn't available everywhere.

terms.plain_definition: Treatments for severe, treatment-resistant depression given under medical supervision, which can work within hours or days. Esketamine is a nasal spray licensed in several countries.
terms.everyday_example: A clinic session with monitoring for a couple of hours afterwards.
terms.common_misunderstanding: This is not the same as recreational ketamine. Clinic use is controlled, monitored, and not for everyone.

terms.plain_definition: An area of research where substances like psilocybin or MDMA are given in a clinical setting alongside therapy, for depression, PTSD, and other conditions. Approval status varies by country and is changing.
terms.everyday_example: A clinical trial with screening, preparation sessions, supervised dosing, and follow-up therapy.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Results are promising but early, and self-medicating with illegal substances is not the same as a trial. This project doesn't give sourcing or dosing information.

terms.plain_definition: A medical doctor who specializes in mental health. Psychiatrists can diagnose, prescribe and monitor medication, and some offer therapy.
terms.everyday_example: The person who reviews your medication every few months.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A psychiatrist isn't 'for serious cases only'. In many systems they're the ones who manage medication for anyone.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: A professional with advanced training in understanding the mind and behaviour, who does assessments and therapy. In most countries they don't prescribe medication.
terms.everyday_example: The person who does a two-hour ADHD assessment, or who sees you weekly for therapy.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Psychologist' and 'psychiatrist' are often mixed up. Psychiatrist = doctor who prescribes; psychologist = assessment and therapy specialist.

terms.plain_definition: General words for trained professionals who provide talking therapy. Titles and licences vary by country, so check qualifications and registration.
terms.everyday_example: A registered counsellor at a community service seeing you fortnightly.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Therapist' isn't a protected title everywhere. Look for registration with a recognized professional body.

terms.plain_definition: A professional who helps with the practical and social side of mental health: housing, benefits, safeguarding, family support, and often therapy.
terms.everyday_example: The person who helps you apply for housing support while you recover.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Social workers aren't only about child protection. In mental health teams they're often the main point of contact.

terms.plain_definition: Nurses with mental health training who provide care, monitoring, and often therapy. In some countries, nurse practitioners can also prescribe.
terms.everyday_example: A community nurse who visits weekly during a difficult patch.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Nurses are often the professional people see most. They're not 'less than' doctors; they're a different role.

terms.plain_definition: Usually the first stop. A GP can diagnose common conditions, start treatment, prescribe many medications, and refer to specialists.
terms.everyday_example: Booking a double appointment to talk about low mood.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Seeing a GP about mental health is normal; a large share of GP appointments involve it. You don't need to be in crisis.

terms.plain_definition: The named person in a mental health team who keeps your care joined up, knows your plan, and is your main contact.
terms.everyday_example: One person to call who knows your history, your medication, and who else is involved.
terms.common_misunderstanding: If you don't know who your care coordinator is, ask. Having one is often a right, not a favour.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: A professional who helps people do the everyday activities that matter to them: routines, work, self-care, sensory needs, and skills.
terms.everyday_example: An OT helping someone with psychosis rebuild a daily structure, or an autistic child with sensory strategies.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Occupational' doesn't just mean jobs. It means anything that occupies your time.

terms.plain_definition: A free phone, text, or chat service you can contact when you're in distress or thinking about suicide, any time, without needing to be 'bad enough'.
terms.everyday_example: Texting a crisis line at 3 a.m. because the thoughts won't stop.
terms.common_misunderstanding: You don't have to be suicidal to call. Crisis lines are for any overwhelming moment, and they're also for people worried about someone else.

terms.plain_definition: A peer-run phone or chat line for support before things reach crisis. Less urgent than a crisis line, often staffed by people with lived experience.
terms.everyday_example: Calling to talk through a lonely evening, not an emergency.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Warmlines fill the gap between 'fine' and 'crisis'. They exist in many US states and some other countries.

also_called: crisis resolution and home treatment team
terms.plain_definition: A team that can come to you, or see you quickly, during a mental health crisis, as an alternative to hospital.
terms.everyday_example: A nurse and a social worker visiting at home twice a day for a week.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Crisis teams aren't only for psychosis. They're for anyone who might otherwise need hospital.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Staying in hospital for mental health treatment, usually for a short period during a crisis, to keep someone safe and start or adjust treatment.
terms.everyday_example: A two-week admission after a severe manic episode.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Admission isn't a failure or a life sentence. Most stays are short, and most are voluntary.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Treatment while living at home: appointments with a clinic, therapist, or team.
terms.everyday_example: Seeing a psychiatrist monthly and a therapist weekly.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Most mental health care is outpatient. Hospital is the exception, not the rule.

terms.plain_definition: Structured treatment for several hours a day, several days a week, while sleeping at home. A step between hospital and ordinary outpatient care.
terms.everyday_example: Five days a week of groups and therapy for a month after leaving hospital.
terms.common_misunderstanding: These programmes exist mainly in the US and some other countries. Elsewhere, crisis teams and day services play a similar role.

terms.plain_definition: Specialist teams for young people in the first few years of psychosis, offering therapy, medication, family support, and help with work or study. Strong evidence for better outcomes.
terms.everyday_example: A 17-year-old and their family supported by one team for three years.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Getting referred early is one of the best things that can happen after a first episode. Don't wait to see if it passes.

terms.plain_definition: Intensive team-based support for people with severe mental illness who find it hard to engage with standard services, with frequent contact and practical help.
terms.everyday_example: A team that visits several times a week and helps with medication, benefits, and housing.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's not surveillance. It's a way of bringing care to people instead of waiting for them to come to clinics.

terms.plain_definition: Therapy or psychiatric appointments by video, phone, or messaging. Evidence shows it works about as well as in-person for many conditions.
terms.everyday_example: Weekly video therapy from your bedroom because the nearest clinic is two hours away.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Check that online providers use licensed professionals. Unregulated apps and 'coaches' aren't the same thing.

terms.plain_definition: The queue for assessment or treatment. Waits can be long, especially for autism and ADHD assessments and for specialist therapy.
terms.everyday_example: Eighteen months for an adult ADHD assessment.
terms.common_misunderstanding: While waiting, you can still ask for interim support, self-help resources, peer groups, and a review if things get worse.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: When a condition hasn't improved enough after trying the standard treatments properly. It's a signal to try different approaches, not a dead end.
terms.everyday_example: Depression that hasn't lifted after two different antidepressants at a full dose for enough time.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Treatment-resistant' is a clinical term, not a verdict. Many options remain, including combinations, therapy, and brain stimulation treatments.

terms.plain_definition: A treatment shown to work in good-quality research, usually several studies compared with placebo or another treatment.
terms.everyday_example: CBT for panic disorder, ERP for OCD, lithium for bipolar disorder.
terms.common_misunderstanding: 'Evidence-based' doesn't mean it works for everyone, and 'not yet evidence-based' doesn't mean useless. It means we have, or don't yet have, good proof.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: A dummy treatment used in research to compare against the real one. The 'placebo effect' is improvement from expectation, care, and attention, which is real and part of all treatment.
terms.everyday_example: People in the sugar-pill group of a trial improving, because being cared for helps.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Responding to placebo doesn't mean your illness is fake. It means hope and care are powerful.

terms.plain_definition: A system where you start with the least intensive treatment likely to help (like guided self-help) and step up if needed.
terms.everyday_example: An online CBT course first; if it isn't enough, face-to-face therapy; then a specialist.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Starting at a low step isn't being fobbed off, as long as stepping up happens when needed. Ask what the next step is.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: England's free service for anxiety and depression, which you can refer yourself to without a GP. Offers CBT, counselling, and online courses.
terms.everyday_example: Filling in a web form and getting an assessment call within a few weeks.
terms.common_misunderstanding: You don't need a diagnosis or a GP letter. Self-referral is the point.

terms.plain_definition: In Australia, a GP can create a plan that gives Medicare rebates for sessions with a psychologist or other provider.
terms.everyday_example: Seeing a GP, getting a plan, and booking a psychologist with a rebate.
terms.common_misunderstanding: The number of rebated sessions changes over time; check the current rules.

terms.plain_definition: India's free, 24/7 national tele-mental-health service, run by the Ministry of Health, offering counselling and referrals in many languages.
terms.everyday_example: Calling the Tele-MANAS number from anywhere in India to speak to a counsellor.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's a government service and free. It can be a first step when private care is out of reach.

sources.title: Tele-MANAS
sources.publisher: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

terms.plain_definition: The first in-depth appointment where a clinician asks about your history, symptoms, life, and goals to work out what's going on and what might help.
terms.everyday_example: An hour of questions about mood, sleep, family history, and what you want to change.
terms.common_misunderstanding: An assessment isn't a test you can fail, and you can bring notes or a friend.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: Short questionnaires (like the PHQ-9 for depression or GAD-7 for anxiety) used to check for likely problems and track change. They are not diagnoses.
terms.everyday_example: Scoring high on an online depression quiz and taking it to your GP.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A score on a screening tool is a starting point for a conversation, never a diagnosis. Only a clinician can make one.

terms.plain_definition: A shared story, built with your clinician, of how your difficulties developed and what keeps them going. Some clinicians use it alongside or instead of a diagnosis.
terms.everyday_example: 'Growing up with a critical parent taught you to expect rejection, so you avoid closeness, which leaves you lonely.'
terms.common_misunderstanding: A formulation is personal in a way a diagnosis can't be. You can ask for one.

terms.plain_definition: A clinician's conclusion that your experiences match a recognized condition. It opens doors to treatment and support, and it's a tool, not a definition of you.
terms.everyday_example: Being told 'this is bipolar II' after years of unexplained ups and downs.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A diagnosis can change over time and can be wrong. It's a best fit at a point in time, and you can ask questions about it.

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision)
A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: A written plan, made when well, about what helps and what doesn't during a crisis: early signs, who to call, what to avoid, what treatments you want.
terms.everyday_example: A card in your wallet with your care coordinator's number and 'please don't shout at me'.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Making a plan isn't expecting the worst. It's making sure your voice is heard when you can't speak up.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health
Wellness Recovery Action Plan (WRAP)
sources.publisher: Advocates for Human Potential / Copeland Center

terms.plain_definition: A short, personal, step-by-step plan for getting through suicidal thoughts: warning signs, things that help, people and places that distract, who to call, and making your surroundings safer.
terms.everyday_example: A note on your phone listing three friends, a crisis number, and 'go to the park' for when the thoughts start.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A safety plan is not a promise contract. It's a practical tool, made with a clinician or on your own, and it saves lives.

sources.title: Build a Safety Plan (988 resource video)

terms.plain_definition: A self-written plan developed by Mary Ellen Copeland that covers daily wellness tools, triggers, early warning signs, and crisis and post-crisis plans.
terms.everyday_example: A folder listing what a good day looks like and what to do when things slip.
terms.common_misunderstanding: WRAP is peer-developed and free to make yourself; some areas run courses.

sources.title: Wellness Recovery Action Plan (WRAP)
sources.publisher: Advocates for Human Potential / Copeland Center

terms.plain_definition: Daily habits that support sleep: regular times, a dark cool room, less screen and caffeine late, no lying awake in bed.
terms.everyday_example: Keeping the same wake time at weekends.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Sleep hygiene alone rarely fixes long-term insomnia. It's the foundation; CBT-I is the treatment.

terms.plain_definition: Regular physical activity has good evidence for easing mild to moderate depression and anxiety, and supports sleep. It's a supplement to care, not a replacement.
terms.everyday_example: A daily twenty-minute walk making the afternoons less heavy.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Telling a depressed person to 'just exercise' misses that depression takes away the ability to start. Small, supported steps work better.

sources.title: Mental health and behavioural conditions guidance

terms.plain_definition: Your right to understand a treatment, its benefits, risks, and alternatives, and to say yes or no freely, before it happens.
terms.everyday_example: A psychiatrist explaining what a medicine does, its side effects, and other options, and you deciding.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Consent isn't a one-time signature. You can ask questions at any point and change your mind.

terms.plain_definition: What you tell a mental health professional stays private. They can't share it with family, employers, or schools without your permission, with a few legal exceptions.
terms.everyday_example: Your therapist won't tell your parents what you said, unless there's a safety reason.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Fear of information leaking stops many people seeking help. Ask your clinician to explain their confidentiality rules at the first session; they should offer anyway.

sources.title: HIPAA Privacy Rule and Sharing Information Related to Mental Health
sources.publisher: US Department of Health and Human Services

terms.plain_definition: The exceptions: professionals may have to share information if you're at serious risk of harming yourself or someone else, if a child or vulnerable adult is being harmed, or if a court orders it. Rules vary by country.
terms.everyday_example: A therapist contacting a crisis team because a client has a plan to end their life.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Talking about suicidal thoughts does not automatically mean being hospitalized. Sharing is usually a last resort and done with you where possible.

sources.title: HIPAA Privacy Rule and Sharing Information Related to Mental Health
sources.publisher: US Department of Health and Human Services

terms.plain_definition: The ability to understand, weigh up, and communicate a decision. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific: someone may lack it for one choice during a crisis and have it for everything else.
terms.everyday_example: A person in severe psychosis may temporarily be unable to weigh up a treatment decision.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Having a mental illness does not mean lacking capacity. The law presumes you have it unless shown otherwise.

terms.plain_definition: Whether a person under 18 can agree to treatment without a parent. In many places a mature young person can, and confidentiality applies; the exact age and rules vary by country and state.
terms.everyday_example: A 16-year-old seeing a school counsellor without their parents being told.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Young people often think help means parents will find out everything. Ask the service what they will and won't share; the answer is usually reassuring.

terms.plain_definition: A document you write when well, saying what treatment you do and don't want if you become too unwell to decide. Its legal force varies: binding in some places, 'must be considered' in others.
terms.everyday_example: 'If I become manic, please contact my sister and do not give me medicine X, which made me worse.'
terms.common_misunderstanding: You don't need a lawyer for most versions. Many charities have templates. Give copies to your team and someone you trust.

terms.plain_definition: Being admitted to hospital or treated without agreeing, under mental health law, when someone is judged to be at serious risk and unable to accept help. Every country has safeguards and rights of appeal.
terms.everyday_example: In England, 'being sectioned' under the Mental Health Act; in California, a '5150' 72-hour hold.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's a last resort, not a punishment, and it has strict rules. You keep rights: to be told why, to appeal, to an advocate, and in many places to refuse some treatments.

terms.plain_definition: A principle in mental health law: care should limit a person's freedom as little as possible while keeping them safe.
terms.everyday_example: Trying home treatment with a crisis team before considering hospital.
terms.common_misunderstanding: If you feel more restricted than necessary, you can ask for the reasoning and request a review.

terms.plain_definition: Rights such as being treated with dignity, being informed, being involved in decisions, complaining, seeing your records, and having an interpreter.
terms.everyday_example: Asking for the care plan to be explained in plain language and getting a copy.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Rights exist even when you're very unwell. An advocate can help you use them.

terms.plain_definition: Asking another clinician to review your diagnosis or treatment. In many systems you have a right to request one.
terms.everyday_example: Asking for a second psychiatrist's view after a diagnosis that doesn't feel right.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Asking for a second opinion isn't rude or ungrateful. Good clinicians support it.

terms.plain_definition: Your right to see what's written about you in your health records, usually by a written request. Some parts can be withheld if they would cause serious harm.
terms.everyday_example: Requesting your notes to understand why a diagnosis was made.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Reading your notes can be upsetting or clarifying. You can ask for corrections if something is wrong.

sources.title: HIPAA Privacy Rule and Sharing Information Related to Mental Health
sources.publisher: US Department of Health and Human Services

terms.plain_definition: Changes an employer or school must make so a person with a disability, including a mental health condition, can take part fairly: flexible hours, quiet space, extra time, written instructions.
terms.everyday_example: Permission to work from home on bad days, or extra exam time for ADHD.
terms.common_misunderstanding: You usually have to ask, and you may need to disclose a condition to get them, but you don't have to share every detail.

also_called: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act
terms.plain_definition: Laws that make it illegal to treat people worse because of a disability, including mental health conditions, in work, education, and services. Examples: the Americans with Disabilities Act (US), the Equality Act 2010 (UK), India's RPwD Act 2016.
terms.everyday_example: Being passed over for promotion after disclosing bipolar disorder may be unlawful discrimination.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Mental health conditions count as disabilities under these laws when they have a substantial, long-term effect, even if they come and go.

terms.plain_definition: Formal plans that set out the support a student with additional needs gets at school. Names differ: IEP and 504 plans (US), EHCP and SEN support (England), individual learning plans elsewhere.
terms.everyday_example: A plan giving a dyslexic student a laptop and extra time in exams.
terms.common_misunderstanding: A plan is a right, not a favour, and parents and students can ask for one to be reviewed.

terms.plain_definition: Therapy fees adjusted to what you can afford. Many private therapists and training clinics offer some sliding-scale places.
terms.everyday_example: Paying a reduced rate because you're a student.
terms.common_misunderstanding: It's normal to ask about sliding-scale options, and it doesn't mean worse care.

terms.plain_definition: Laws, such as the US federal parity act, requiring insurance to cover mental health and substance use care on the same terms as physical health.
terms.everyday_example: An insurer can't set a lower session limit for therapy than for physiotherapy.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Parity is often not enforced well. If you're denied coverage, you can appeal and complain to the regulator.

terms.plain_definition: A free, confidential service some employers provide, usually a few counselling sessions and a helpline.
terms.everyday_example: Six free sessions through work after a bereavement.
terms.common_misunderstanding: EAPs are confidential; your employer isn't told you used it. Sessions are limited, so ask about onward referral.

terms.plain_definition: Time off work for a mental health condition, usually with a note from a doctor. Mental health is as valid a reason as physical health.
terms.everyday_example: A GP note for two weeks off for depression, with a phased return.
terms.common_misunderstanding: You don't have to tell your employer the diagnosis in most places; 'a medical condition' is usually enough.

terms.plain_definition: Someone independent of your care team who helps you understand your rights, speak up, and be heard, especially in hospital or under mental health law.
terms.everyday_example: An advocate attending a ward review with you and making sure your views are recorded.
terms.common_misunderstanding: An advocate is on your side, not the hospital's. In some countries you have a legal right to one.

terms.plain_definition: People who support someone with a mental health condition often have rights to information (with the person's consent), to a carer's assessment, and to support for themselves.
terms.everyday_example: A parent asking for a carer's assessment while supporting an adult child with schizophrenia.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Confidentiality limits what services can tell you, but it doesn't stop them listening to you or supporting you.

terms.plain_definition: Legal arrangements where someone else makes certain decisions for a person who lacks capacity. Power of attorney is chosen by the person in advance; guardianship or conservatorship is imposed by a court.
terms.everyday_example: An adult child managing a parent's finances after dementia advances.
terms.common_misunderstanding: These should be the least restrictive possible and only for decisions the person can't make. They are not automatic with any diagnosis.

terms.plain_definition: Laws that control how your health information is stored and shared. HIPAA in the US and data protection law (GDPR) in the UK and Europe are examples.
terms.everyday_example: A clinic needing your written permission before sending notes to your employer.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Privacy law protects you, but it doesn't stop you sharing your own information, and it allows emergency sharing to keep you safe.

sources.title: HIPAA Privacy Rule and Sharing Information Related to Mental Health
sources.publisher: US Department of Health and Human Services

terms.plain_definition: Negative beliefs and treatment aimed at people with mental health conditions. 'Self-stigma' is when a person turns those beliefs on themselves. Stigma stops people getting help.
terms.everyday_example: Not telling anyone about a diagnosis for fear of being seen as weak or dangerous.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Stigma is a social problem, not a personal one. It shrinks when people talk openly and when language changes.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: First-hand experience of mental health difficulties or of caring for someone. Increasingly valued in designing services, research, and peer support.
terms.everyday_example: A person with lived experience of psychosis co-designing a new crisis service.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Lived experience is expertise. It doesn't replace clinical knowledge; it complements it.

sources.title: A to Z of mental health

terms.plain_definition: 'Person with schizophrenia' (person-first) puts the person before the condition. 'Autistic person' (identity-first) treats the condition as part of identity. Communities differ on which they prefer.
terms.everyday_example: Many autistic adults prefer 'autistic'; most people with depression prefer 'person with depression'.
terms.common_misunderstanding: There's no single right answer. When in doubt, ask the person, and follow what their community generally prefers.

terms.plain_definition: Guidelines for talking and writing about suicide in ways that reduce risk: no methods or locations, no 'committed', no simple explanations, always include help information.
terms.everyday_example: A news story that says 'died by suicide' and ends with a helpline number.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Talking about suicide safely helps. It's unsafe detail, not the topic itself, that causes harm.

terms.plain_definition: If care goes wrong, you can complain to the service, and then to an independent body (such as an ombudsman or health regulator). Services must respond.
terms.everyday_example: Writing to a hospital after a dismissive crisis assessment and getting a formal response.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Complaining shouldn't affect your care, and an advocate can help you do it.
